svg.aria-label: Diagram: the three kinds of Google Cloud IAM role, the split between the current basic roles and the legacy basic roles, the two behavioural differences between them, the console asymmetry that blocks granting the replacements, and the maintenance trade between predefined and custom roles
svg.title: IAM roles: a taxonomy that quietly changed, and a console that still offers only the leaky half
svg.text: Owner, Editor and Viewer are now the legacy basic roles. The rename is not cosmetic.
Two things behave differently, and both change how you scope a grant and how you audit one.
Basic roles — Admin, Writer, Reader
Thousands of permissions, across all services.
Can carry IAM conditions.
Contain all the access they confer.
But: Preview, under the Pre-GA Offerings Terms.
And: cannot be granted from the console at all.
API, gcloud, or a PAM entitlement only.
Legacy basic — Owner, Editor, Viewer
Predate IAM. Originally known as primitive roles.
Cannot carry conditions on their bindings.
Grant permissions that are NOT in the role —
services add more for anyone holding one.
Cloud Storage convenience values and BigQuery
special group membership are the examples.
These CAN be granted from the console.
So the path of least resistance still leads to the worse role
The roles with the known defect are clickable. The roles that fix it are not. A team that grants by clicking keeps
producing legacy bindings without ever choosing to. Post #28: the console is not the documentation.
Predefined — the default
Granular, scoped to a service, managed by Google.
Google updates the permissions as necessary,
such as when new features or services arrive.
Which you will not notice: the ETag is always
AA==, so the role has no version identity.
Custom — exactly what you list
Up to 3,000 permissions. 300 per org, 300 per project.
No folder level — define at the organization instead.
Not maintained by Google. Nothing updates them
when services change — that is now your job.
Whoever may EDIT one holds unlimited access.
The trade is not breadth — it is who carries the role forward
A predefined role drifts wider without telling you. A custom role stays exactly as narrow as the day you wrote it.
Neither column is the safe one: one fails as quiet scope creep, the other as access that stops working.
Google still recommends predefined first — drift you do not control beats a permission set nobody owns.
What the rename admits
You could read Owner’s permission list in full and still be wrong about what the grant allowed. Admin, Writer
and Reader are the same breadth with that property removed, plus the ability to carry a condition.
Audit legacy basic bindings first. They are the ones you cannot audit by reading the role.
The right move is not to chase the new basic roles.
It is to stop granting broad roles at all — the recommendation before the rename, and the one thing it does not change.
